items.question: How soon can you start?
items.answer: Usually within three weeks. Discovery sprints are the quickest to schedule because they are short and self-contained.

items.question: Do you work with our engineers or replace them?
items.answer: With them. We prefer to pair with your team so that the knowledge stays with you after we leave.

items.question: What if the sprint says we should not build the thing?
items.answer: Then you saved the cost of building it. We would rather give you a clear no than a polished yes.

items.question: Do you sign NDAs?
items.answer: Yes, on request, before we talk about anything confidential.

blocks.heading: A small studio on purpose
blocks.body:
Fernlight started in a spare room in 2017 with two people and a whiteboard. We are still small, because small teams talk to each other and big ones talk to calendars.

We turn down more work than we take. That is how we keep the senior people on your project, from the first call to the last release.

posts.title: Why your first prototype should be embarrassing
posts.excerpt: A rough prototype gets honest feedback in a day. A polished one gets polite feedback in a month.
posts.alt: Overlapping circles and arcs in violet, pink and amber
posts.body:
People are kind to things that look finished. Show them a beautiful mock-up and they will say it looks great. Show them a scribble and they will tell you what is wrong with the idea.

## Make it just real enough

A good first prototype has three properties:

- It takes under a day to make.
- It has real words in it, not placeholder text.
- Someone outside the team can click through it unaided.

## Then watch, do not explain

Sit next to a person while they use it and say nothing. Every question they ask out loud is a gap in the design.

> If you are not slightly embarrassed by the prototype, you spent too long on it.

posts.title: The one-page measures sheet
posts.excerpt: Five numbers, agreed before launch, written in words. Here is the template we use.
posts.alt: Rising bars and a line in teal and violet
posts.body:
Dashboards multiply. Decisions do not. The cure is a single page that lists the few measures a product lives or dies by.

## What goes on the page

1. The behaviour you want more of.
2. The behaviour you want less of.
3. A guardrail, so that you do not win one number by breaking another.

Write each measure as a sentence: *new customers who finish setup in their first week*. If you cannot write it as a sentence, you do not understand it yet.

## Review it monthly

One meeting, one page, ten minutes of silence to read it first.

posts.title: Handing off design without losing the plot
posts.excerpt: The handoff is not a file transfer. It is a conversation that starts on day one.
posts.alt: Tilted rounded shapes moving left to right
posts.body:
A design that arrives in engineering as a surprise is a design that will be rebuilt. Bring the engineers into the room early and the 'handoff' shrinks to a formality.

## Three habits that help

- Name components the way the code names them.
- Draw the empty, loading and error states first.
- Review the build against the design together, in the browser, not from screenshots.

posts.title: Quiet software for loud days
posts.excerpt: Notes on designing for the moment someone is tired, distracted and holding a phone in one hand.
posts.alt: A grid of dots that fades out
posts.body:
Most interfaces are designed for the best version of the user: rested, attentive, two hands free. Most use happens at the worst version.

## Design for the worst moment

- Make the main action reachable with a thumb.
- Never ask the same question twice.
- Let people leave and come back exactly where they were.

Quiet software does not mean boring software. It means software that does not demand attention it has not earned.
